Yes. Russia has held the initiative ever since Kursk. Or since the 2023 counteroffensive, if you want to count Kursk as an exception. 

In the West they keep talking about Russian offensives, but they aren’t Western style big arrow offensives in the conventional sense. Rather they are the product of attritional pressure. Ukraine doesn’t have enough reserves to stabilize the entire front line, so Russia applies pressure everywhere. When a section of the Ukrainian line becomes weakened and combat ineffective, Russian pressure begins to roll the line westwards. Ukraine then realizes it is losing ground and scrapes together forces from what is already deployed to throw at the crumbling part of the front. That renewed pressure meets the Russian pressure and the front stabilizes in that area. The problem is in doing this Ukraine weakened some other area and the Russian pressure in that area becomes greater than the Ukrainian pressure in that area. Russia doesn’t have goals of taking some specific points for strategic results. The point of moving forward when the pressure is in the Russian favor is to keep the Ukrainian Army engaged in combat along a wide front, stretched thin, and suffering losses. 

It’s been pretty clear for a while now that Ukrainian conscription is not enough to replace losses and form a new reserve force. It’s been slowly climbing up from 350,000 to 500,000, but the Russian side has been growing even faster. There are currently three Russian army formations in Ukraine and only one of the three is regularly taking part in combat. Much of the newest equipment is going to the units not participating in the war right now, including T-90M, T-90A, and T-72B3 tanks equipped with Arena-M. 

There will almost certainly be a big arrow offensive with one or both of those Russian armies in reserve within the next year. That will be when Russia finally moves on from attrition to taking territory.

Also, by default, the 2.4 GHz wifi signal data protocol on a Mavic drone is direct sequence spread spectrum, thereby inherently jam resistant. Frequency hopping is a very "duh" strategy to enhance jam resistance, so that tactic is nothing the Russians would have not thought through, yet not actually planned for. The Israel situation is a weird one for me. I'm not a fan of this kind of preemptive operations - but equally I am well aware that the necessary intelligence to cause an operation like this to be launched for good reason will not and should not be shared with civilians until a long time after the operation has concluded. Israel are more brutal than I would like, but equally, they are in a situation where the consequences of failure for them are quite literally genocidal. Hamas, Iran, and Iran's other proxies are very open about their genocidal ambitions. Ergo, it's hard for me to criticise their actions in Gaza without a credible alternative being presented for them to deal with Hamas. At the moment, the people who are (/claim to be) horrified at what is happening in Gaza seem to think that doing nothing is a credible alternative. It isn't, and doing so just makes you look like a malicious actor. Israel can't afford to let Hamas escape with impunity (except, perhaps, if Iran itself falls) and so if you want Israel to stop, we need to hear some constructive other way of dealing with bringing Hamas to justice, and returning as many of the hostages that remain alive as possible.

As regards Iran specifically, anyone who thinks that Israel are morally worse in comparison to Iran are just ignorant, so I will always back Israel over Iran in a conflict even if I am sceptical as to just how close Iran are to gaining nukes, and we won't know how credible the information appeared to Israel leading up to this attack for quite a while. It's just brutal pragmatism, there. If one of the two states has to go, then the world would be far more safe without Iran than it would without Israel. (Equally, as far as I am concerned, Israel and Iran have been at war since October last year, even if it has not been as full-blown as it currently is now, so labelling this as Israel starting the fight - as their enemies have been doing - is just deliberately mendacious.)

4:52 To clarifye on thing: the reactor of Fukushima was not active when the nuclear desaster happened. During the earthquake, the reactor shut down by itself. The incident was, that the facility ran out of electrical power and the old, used fuel rods which were stored for cooling down could not be cooled anymore without electricity. The Treaty of Geneva, more specifically the 1949 Geneva Conventions, is a set of international treaties that establish rules for the treatment of civilians and combatants during wartime. These treaties, adopted in 1949, are the foundation of modern international humanitarian law and protect those who are not taking part in hostilities, such as civilians, and those who are no longer fighting, such as prisoners of war. 
Key aspects of the Geneva Conventions:
Protection of Civilians:
The Conventions protect civilians, including those in occupied territories, from violence, torture, and discrimination based on race, religion, or political opinion. 
Treatment of Prisoners of War:
The Conventions define the rights and protections for prisoners of war, including their treatment, working conditions, and right to communication with neutral states. 
Protection of Wounded and Sick:
The Conventions ensure the humane treatment of wounded and sick soldiers, both on land and at sea. 
Additional Protocols:
In 1977, two additional protocols were adopted to expand the protections of the Geneva Conventions, particularly in the context of non-international armed conflicts. 
History and Significance:
The Geneva Conventions were developed and updated over time, with the first convention in 1864 focusing on the treatment of wounded soldiers. The 1949 conventions, in particular, were a response to the atrocities of World War II and have served as a crucial framework for international humanitarian law ever since.

comment_text: The laser weapons are most impressive to me. I remember 20 years ago or so they were testing experimental chemical laser platforms and they weren't very practical. They were massively heavy high power lasers but used loads of fuel to operate. Several tonnes to reach peak output and fire a single shot. They could only do a few shots because of all the fuel you needed to carry around, produced nasty gases and lacked the sensors and control to hit multiple targets. The idea was to hit ICBMs in boost phase, but you were never getting close enough fast enough. Here we are 20 years later and smaller solid state laser weapons are being tested to hit drones and missiles and they show great promise. They actually work. They are compact, can be fired repeatedly and their power output is increasing with development. The future will definitely have laser weapons in it.

This evolution of the tactical picture very much resembles the evolution of trench warfare in the First World War. When trenches were first established both sides packed them with  men right in contact with the opponent. What happened was those packed trenches just became targets for the artillery. By 1917 the front line was little more than a series of outposts, basically shell holes, while the real line of resistance was three or more kilometers back- out of range of the heavy artillery. Any advance would be met by a prompt counterattack, which the attacking force would be hard pressed to resist.

Both sides found solutions to the problem: the Germans invented infiltration tactics, while the allies invented tanks. 

By summer 1918 offence was possible again.

From the sounds of it Ukraine is evolving into a scenario where it will be 1915 again: a sufficient density of drones will mean no offence is possible.

At which point one would sincerely hope the Russians would just give up and end this thing.
